content_voiceover: This is a Blood journal image case, a seven-year-old boy of Pakistani origin referred for thrombocytopenia with an incidental note of possible IgA deficiency. The peripheral smear shows a markedly enlarged platelet, approaching the size of a small lymphocyte, but notably pale and gray rather than displaying the normal fine purple granularity of a healthy platelet. That pale, agranular appearance on Wright stain is the morphologic hallmark of Gray Platelet Syndrome, an inherited macrothrombocytopenia caused by biallelic NBEAL2 mutations, which impair packaging of proteins into platelet alpha granules. Alpha granules normally store von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, and growth factors like PDGF and TGF-beta, so their absence produces the gray color and mild to moderate mucocutaneous bleeding. The IgA deficiency mentioned here is an incidental association, not part of the diagnostic criteria. Board pearl, the size plus color together point to a specific diagnosis, not just generic macrothrombocytopenia.
keypoints: Giant, pale gray platelets on smear = alpha-granule deficiency
Gray Platelet Syndrome: NBEAL2 mutation, autosomal recessive
Alpha granules store VWF, fibrinogen, PDGF, TGF-beta
Distinguish from Bernard-Soulier and MYH9 disorders by gray color
keypoint_voiceover: A giant, pale gray platelet on a Wright-stained smear is the signature of Gray Platelet Syndrome, caused by autosomal recessive NBEAL2 mutations that block alpha-granule packaging. Since alpha granules carry von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, and growth factors, their absence produces both the gray color and a mild bleeding tendency. The color, not just the size, is what separates this from other giant platelet disorders.
